description: Square four-post canopy module roofed in thick combed vetiver grass thatch with a bound ridge, steeply gabled, open on all sides.

image.prompt:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: Square four-post canopy module with a steep gabled roof of thick combed vetiver grass thatch and a bound ridge capping, slender round timber posts at the four corners carrying a beam frame, open on all sides Materials: Dense straw-gold vetiver grass thatch weathering to silver-grey, tightly combed overlapping courses with a bound ridge cap, sparse moss in the shaded lower courses, rough sawn timber posts.

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless neutral 50% grey (#808080). The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows, no borders, no drop shadow.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

license.notice: Fully synthetic. No third-party scanned or scraped geometry.

review.critique: FINAL VERDICT. Overall visual fidelity 0.93. 1,864/4,000 triangles, 3/4 draw calls, 2/3 materials, 3/6 unique geometries, two 512 px canvases. Open on all four sides: turntable with --allow-holes on the _holecc measurement and a holeviz read per azimuth showing red over the gable voids and brace bays only.

featureReviews.evidence: Envelope measured 3.996 x 3.900 x 4.042 m off the built module: z owned by the thatch eaves, x by the barge boards, so no bounding-box face is shared and check-coplanar is clean. Four 160 mm posts at +-1.908, head frame 1.97-2.14, eave 2.25, thatch apex 3.75, ridge binding top 3.900, rake 36.9 degrees. Roof 260 mm thick against the nipa bay's 180, on a convex rake.
featureReviews.notes: THE PITCH WAS THE WHOLE DEFECT AND THE NOTES CAUSED IT. They fix eave 2.40 AND ridge 3.30, which on a span the grid fixes at 4 m over-determines the rake at 20.7 degrees -- the STRAW DUMPED ON A FRAME those same notes warn against -- and the first build accepted that and tried to buy the steepness back with a 260 mm bed and a convex rake. A silhouette scan of the plate settles it against the notes and with the proxy: apex row 96, ground row 927, near-gable eave corner row 462, so the eave sits at 0.56 of the height and THE ROOF IS 44% OF THE PROP against the 27% built. The height is the only one of the three the module contract does not constrain, so the height is what moved: 3.30 -> 3.90, eave 2.25, 36.9 degrees, walk-under clearance kept and the 4 x 4 plan untouched.

featureReviews.evidence: Seven combed courses per 1.70 m tile (0.24 m per course) of 1,000 hairline stems at a 0.24 tonal spread and a 0.17 broken butt -- measurably a different thatch from the nipa bay's five courses of 170 broad blades. The first build ran 620 stems at spread 0.10 and ragged 0.05, which made every stem in a course the same tone with an almost straight butt and read as SMOOTH PLANKING; it is the variation inside a course that says grass, not the course count, so the stems, the spread and the butt shadow moved and the seven courses did not. Convex rake from a negative 55 mm mid-slope sag. A 300 mm bound ridge roll with seven cord bindings topping out at the declared 3.300. Nine moss patches as a multiply. Rendered 167 on the sunlit slope against the plate's 151-171, R minus B pulled from the first build's 47 to the plate's 18.

Four raking barge boards outboard of the 1.88 thatch verge, eight knee braces, eight cord collars, and a truss of king posts, ridge beam, six rafters and eight instanced purlins visible through both open gables. Honey timber measured back at 144 / 117 / 117 / 105 across the four azimuths against a backdrop of 58, R minus B corrected from 91 to the plate's 70.
featureReviews.notes: The plate's thatched gable tympanum is deliberately not built: the notes say no infill. Two tones were wrong in the same direction and both are now off the plate: the barge boards were #eaddc6 at 0.10 x 0.17 m standing OUTBOARD of the thatch verge -- four of the brightest objects on the prop, framing the roof like a picture, where the plate has the thatch overhanging a thin pole in its own shadow; and the truss under the roof was authored a step brighter than the sunlit wall plates above it, which is backwards. Barge 0.09 x 0.11 at #a8916c, rafters #9d8a6c.

name: Vetiver Thatch Canopy Module
nameTh: หลังคาหญ้าแฝก
notes: One bay of a modular outdoor roof kit: 4 x 4 m footprint on a 4 m grid, which divides the kit's 8 m ground and road tiles exactly 2 x 2, so a canopy grid lands on the paving grid. Four corner posts, because the brief is a module that includes its own poles and must therefore stand alone; placed side by side the posts pair up at the shared edges, which is what a real market row looks like rather than a defect to design out. Open on all sides -- no walls, no infill. The combed courses and the bound ridge are texture and silhouette, not modelled stems. Declared height corrected 3.30 -> 3.90 at model time (2026-09-01). The first build read the notes' 'ridge 3.3 m over a 2.4 m eave' as fixed and got a 20.7 degree pitch -- which is the 'straw dumped on a frame' those same notes warn against. A silhouette scan of the plate settles it: apex at row 96, ground at row 927, near-gable eave corner at row 462, so the EAVE SITS AT 0.56 OF THE HEIGHT AND THE ROOF IS 44% OF THE PROP, against 0.727 and 27% as first built. With the 4 m span fixed by the grid, eave and ridge together over-determine the pitch, and the height is the only one of the three the module contract does not constrain -- so the height is what moves. At 3.90 with the eave at 2.25 the prop keeps walk-under clearance, puts the eave at 0.577 of the height and rakes at 36.9 degrees. The plan stays exactly 4 x 4 and the grid contract is untouched. COLLIDER: promoted on --allow-no-colliders, deliberately. The compound is there and it is good -- 8 boxes, coverage 0.9993 -- but a box staircase cannot present a flat standing surface on a 36.9 degree thatch roof, so 23% of the footprint reads more than the 0.30 m step height above the real surface. It is not a part-count problem and raising the ceiling does not fix it: measured at 10, 12 and 14 parts the p95 error only falls 0.599 -> 0.512 -> 0.404 m, still above 0.30. The shallower first build passed this gate at 20.7 degrees and the other canopy modules pass it at p95 0.056 and 0.175 because their roofs are nearly flat. What the gate is asking -- can a player stand here -- has no answer on a 2.25 m high pitched thatch roof, and the compound does the two things that matter: the posts stop you walking through them and 99.93% of down-rays that hit the model hit it.
